After getting familiar with what an A/B testing is, let's take a look at how an A/B testing could be conducted!

<span id="制定目标"></span>
## Set goals

<span id="明确北极星目标"></span>
### Identify the North Star target

For any company, whether it is an Internet company or a traditional company, there is one most important business development metric \- "North Star Metric" (North Star Metric), also known as "One Metric That Matters" (OMTM).

Usually North Star Metric needs to include four characteristics:


* It can reflect the core value that the product provides to users.

* Able to measure the level of user activity.

* It is easy to be understood by the team.

* It reflects the overall success of the enterprise.


For some mature industries, North Star Metric has been relatively fixed, such as:


|Core value |North Star Metric |
|---|---|
|Offer users value\-for\-money products and interactive shopping experiences |GMV (gross merchandise volume) |
|Let users get reliable answers efficiently |number of questions answered |
|To provide users with high\-quality household products and life services |number of orders |


Obviously, the development of North Star Metric is a more strategic work for *enterprises* , but A/B testing cannot bypass this link. Under the premise of a clear North Star goal, *enterprises* can achieve rapid iteration and growth through systematic A/B testings.

<span id="细化指标"></span>
### Refined metrics

After identifying the North Star goal, each business team needs to divide its own tasks, which involves breaking down the North Star Metric into actionable metrics. Take the e\-commerce platform as an example, if I set the GMV in 2019 to be $3 million, then we can gradually break this North Star goal down, for example:

<img src="data:image/svg+xml;base64," />

After the North Star Metric is refined, various departments can conduct targeted experiments around the refined specific metrics.

<span id="建立假设"></span>
## Establish hypotheses

Once the goal is clear, the growth team should start analyzing the early data and identify growth opportunities in the data. This process requires product managers, operations managers, and technology developers to jointly discuss and complete.

After the analysis, the team needs to come up with hypotheses, such as: changing the main color of the purchase page from blue to red can increase the user purchase rate by 3%. It is worth noting that the assumptions we make must include two aspects: the first is **to propose a new strategy**, "the main color of the purchase page is changed from blue to red", which determines how we will configure the experimental parameters in the experiment; the second is **the exact improvement value**, such as "the user purchase rate increases by 3%", which determines how many users should enter the experiment.

In A/B testings, using the "expected value and improvement value" of the metric to extrapolate the experimental flow requires complex statistical knowledge. However, even if you don't have the knowledge, using a well\-established A/B testing tool \- BytePlus A/B Testing's "Experimental Traffic Suggestion Tool" feature \- you can easily determine the traffic that should enter the experiment. Please see [Traffic Calculator](https://docs.byteplus.com/docs/DataTester/Traffic-Calculator) for details.

<span id="配置实验"></span>
## Configuration experiment

After the above content is clear, it is time to set up the experiment. Taking A/B testing as an example, to set up a complete experiment, we need to pay attention to the following aspects:

<span id="where-实验开在哪儿"></span>
### Where does the experiment conduct?

The "where to conduct" here refers to how to choose the right experimental layer.

What is the "experimental layer"? The "experimental layer" technology is a traffic stratification technology developed to enable multiple experiments to be parallel without interfering with each other, and to obtain enough traffic.

Imagine that I have four experiments to conduct, each of which requires 30% of the traffic to produce reliable results. In order to run these 4 experiments simultaneously, 4 \* 30% = 120% of the traffic is required, which means that *100%*  of the traffic is not enough to be allocated to these 4 experiments at the same time. So at this point, I can only choose to sort the experiments and let several experiments be completed one after the other. But this will result in inefficient experiments. Imagine that many large Internet companies have tens of thousands of experiments to conduct every year. If they could only wait in line, the experiments could be arranged until 9012.

So is there a way to solve this problem?

Yes, it is to use experimental layer technology to "copy" the overall flow countless times, forming countless flow layers, so that the overall flow can be reused countless times, thereby improving experimental efficiency. The flow between the layers is **orthogonal**, which can be simply understood as: under the premise of choosing the correct flow layer, the flow is scientifically allocated to ensure that the results of each experiment will not be disturbed by the experiments of other layers.

<img src="data:image/svg+xml;base64," />

When selecting the experimental layer, the rule we have to follow is: if the experiment **has a correlation**, then the experiment **must be placed in the same layer**; if the experiment **has no correlation**, then the experiment **can be placed in different layers**.

<span id="when-实验开多久"></span>
### When and for how long?

Based on some statistical principles, too long or too short of an experiment conduction is not conducive to the credibility of the experimental results. Usually the duration of the experiment should be consistent with the "data feature period" of the product. How to understand it? For example, for a *live streaming* app product, the user's *activity* is low from Monday to Friday, and the *activity* is high on weekends. Then experimental periods should usually be set to one week when this *live streaming* product doing A/B testings.

<span id="who-谁进入实验"></span>
### Who entered the experiment

In the experiment, we need to set the amount of traffic entering the experiment. Usually in the initial stages of an experiment, we tend to allocate a smaller amount of traffic (for example: 1%) to the experiment first. If the initial experimental results are all normal, the flow can be further increased; if there is a huge abnormality in the experimental data, the experiment can be terminated at any time. Small traffic minimizes the impact of experimental anomalies on user experience.

In addition to setting the traffic size, we can also add restrictions to filter users entering the experiment, such as only looking at "Android users", only looking at "users in Beijing" and so on. This part of the filter condition usually needs to be confirmed by both the experimental initiator and the analyst.

<span id="metric-关注的指标"></span>
### Metrics to focus on

Determine which metrics are our concern. Let's take a look at the hypothesis we made earlier: changing the main color of the purchase page from blue to red can increase user purchase rates by 3%. In this experiment, "user purchase rate" must be our focus metric, and our "**target metric**." In addition, we should also pay attention to some important data metrics that products often pay attention to, in order to *observe* whether the new strategy in the experiment will have a negative impact on other important metrics.

<span id="how-实验配置参数"></span>
### How to configure experimental parameters

The configuration parameters are actually a string of code that determines how different the product will be to the user who enters the experiment. Using the previous hypothesis as an example, if I assume that "changing the main color of the purchase page from blue to red will increase the user purchase rate", then in the experiment, the configuration parameters I issued should make the purchase page color of the experimental group of users appear red. The specific codes for these parameters need to be confirmed with the development of the product.

<span id="前期测试"></span>
## Pre\-test

After going through the above steps, our experiment is basically set up. But before we rush to start the experiment, we should also conduct preliminary testing of the experiment.

During the test, we will add the "test user" to the whitelist, and *observe* whether the experimental configuration can take effect normally on the test user's mobile phone/computer(such as whether the color change of the purchase page can be displayed normally), whether the client side/webpage will crash, and whether the experimental data can be reported correctly.

> Before the experiment is officially launched, it is usually necessary to select a few users to enter the testing phase to observe whether the experiment can normally obtain the data to be collected, or whether there are bugs on the client side. Users who participate in this step are called "whitelisted users".


<span id="评估结果"></span>
## Evaluation result

The experimental results need to be evaluated from two aspects: the first is the increase and decrease of the data results; the second is to determine whether the data results can be trusted, that is, whether the results are "significant".

The increase and decrease of data is needless to say, how to understand whether the data is significant?

We know that an A/B testing is a kind of low\-traffic test, and we need to take a certain amount of samples from the overall traffic to verify whether the new strategy is effective. During the sampling process, the sample does not fully represent the whole. The uneven distribution of the sample leads to a situation where the experimental results may lead to a situation where the strategy I took actually didn't work, but the experimental results show that the strategy worked.

Statistics tells us that such errors cannot be completely avoided, but we can use some statistical methods to calculate the probability of such errors occurring in the process of obtaining the results of experimental data. In other words, we can determine what percentage of our experiments are reliable.

According to the accepted standards in the industry, in A/B testings, if the experimental data results are statistically reliable with a probability of more than 95%, we shall say that the data results are significant. Such data can be used to determine whether the experimental hypothesis is valid.

In the A/B testing platform, we use the colors in the data report to indicate whether the data is significant.

For ease of judgment, the "A/B testing" directly uses color visualization in the data table to give significance. Green means that the metric is positively significant relative to the control group, red is negatively significant, and black is insignificant.
